body:
Dialogs in the running project or the editor itself?

Are you using single-window mode ("display/window/subwindows/embed_subwindows" project setting)? In this case this is expected since dialogs are not real windows, but controls in the main window.

Thanks for the quick response!

I want to clarify that this issue isn’t tied to a specific project — it affects the entire Godot editor. The root of the problem is that the accessibility tree doesn’t reflect the visual hierarchy of the UI. Because of that, screen readers can’t correctly understand what each control is, how elements relate to each other, or even when a new window appears.

In accessibility-friendly frameworks like Windows UI, Qt, or the web platform, every control exposes its role, its name, and its parent-child structure. That’s what allows a screen reader to immediately recognize when something is a dialog, a panel, a button, a labeled section, and so on. It also makes it possible to know whether a container has children, whether a panel is meant to be a dialog, or whether menus or subpanels are expanded.

Godot’s accessibility tree currently doesn’t provide that consistency, and because of this:

- Screen readers can’t tell when a control contains child elements.
- They can’t recognize when something is supposed to be a dialog window.
- Menus or subpanels don’t expose whether they’re expanded or collapsed.
- And the biggest problem: **screen readers never announce dialog titles**.

This is something I experience every day. When I open any dialog — Editor Settings, Project Settings, Create Node, etc. — the screen reader never announces the title. From the accessibility tree’s perspective, the dialog isn’t exposed as a window at all. It’s just a generic container with no name and no role, so the screen reader has no way to inform the user that a dialog even appeared.

This is why fixing the structure of the accessibility tree is so important. Without the right roles and hierarchy, the interface becomes confusing and unpredictable for anyone relying on assistive technologies. It’s impossible to know where you are, what just opened, or how different UI elements relate to each other.

Improving this would have a huge impact on usability and would make the editor genuinely accessible.

## Additional context on how dialogs and UI roles should be exposed to screen readers

To give a better idea of what the expected behavior should be, here are examples of how a screen reader like NVDA *should* announce dialogs when they appear in Godot:

- “Editor Settings. Dialog.”
- “Project Settings. Dialog.”
- “Create Node. Dialog.”
- “Create Project. Dialog.”

This is standard behavior in platforms with complete accessibility support: the moment a dialog opens, the screen reader gets the role (`dialog`), the accessible name (its title), and the fact that this is the active window the user is now interacting with.

### Why this matters technically

Right now, Godot’s dialogs don’t expose:

- A proper role such as `dialog`.
- A readable name that matches the dialog’s title.
- A clear parent-child structure that identifies it as a window containing other controls.

Because of this, dialogs are indistinguishable from regular containers. The user never knows a dialog appeared; there’s no audible change of context.

### A comparison with UI elements that *do* work well

Some parts of Godot already expose accessibility correctly:

- **Menus** have a consistent hierarchy that screen readers can navigate.
- **Tree views** (like the Scene Tree) expose their structure clearly, allowing proper traversal.

These show that Godot is capable of providing accurate accessibility metadata when there’s a clear hierarchy.

Dialogs, panels, and other containers should follow this same pattern.  
For panels that serve as sections with titles, assigning a role such as `group` helps establish logical separation and makes navigation more intuitive. This is standard across multiple accessibility frameworks.

### Real-world impact

This isn’t theoretical — several blind friends of mine have tried to use the editor, and they all run into the same wall: the interface feels unpredictable because dialogs have no role, no title, and no clear announcement. When they open a dialog, there’s simply no way to know it happened.

This single issue is one of the biggest barriers preventing visually impaired users from learning or adopting Godot.

### Summary

A well-structured accessibility tree with proper roles, names, and hierarchy is essential for screen readers to present a coherent interface. Since menus and trees already show that hierarchical accessibility works in Godot, applying the same logic to dialogs and titled panels would immediately improve the editor’s accessibility in a meaningful way.

I can provide recordings, examples, or additional testing if needed.

Roles and titles should be already set for dialogs, and seems to be working correctly in projects and project manager (at least macOS accessibility inspector show them and screen reader do announce opened dialogs and their titles).

But some of the editor dialogs seems to indeed not identify as such (likely misconfigured as menus). I'll check it.

Note: Currently, very little was done specifically for the editor UI accessibility. UI was designed without any considerations for it and therefore control hierarchy is pretty convoluted. And some parts of the editor use custom UI elements and currently aren't working with accessibility API at all or partially.

Thank you for the follow-up, and let me clarify my point so it’s not misunderstood.
I’m not referring to focus behavior — the initial focus on the first control inside the dialog, the circular navigation, and the fact that the active window is treated correctly are all working perfectly. That part is actually great, and I appreciate how well it’s handled.
What I’m referring to is purely the semantic accessibility structure of dialogs on Windows.
I work with NVDA daily, both as a regular user and as an accessibility professional (web, desktop, and mobile), so I’m describing this from both perspectives.
Even though dialogs visually behave correctly, the dialog container itself does not appear with a proper role="dialog" in the accessibility tree on Windows. All internal controls (labels, buttons, etc.) appear as children of the main window, not as children of an accessible dialog node.
So even if the dialog role is assigned somewhere internally, it is not being reflected in the final accessibility tree delivered to AccessKit on Windows.
This makes dialogs functionally usable but semantically invisible to screen-reader users. The user does not get any announcement like “Dialog: <title>”, and the context of being inside a dialog is completely missing unless they already know the UI by memory. This becomes especially uncomfortable or confusing for players of exported games or for new developers trying Godot with a screen reader.
I’m trying to help strengthen the current partial accessibility support by reporting every issue I find while using Godot daily. I truly want the engine to grow, and proper dialog semantics are an important part of accessible UI patterns.
Thanks again for looking into this — I really appreciate the effort.

Hi, please note that support for dialogs was added in https://github.com/AccessKit/accesskit/pull/549 which will only be in the next version. It will take a bit of time to publish new C bindings and update Godot.
Okay, thank you very much for responding. So, I'll be waiting for when it's implemented.
